verdict.root_cause: At 03:54:12 UTC a platform-automation principal attached a traffic-shaping container to the cart-service network namespace applying a fixed 300ms, zero-jitter egress delay on eth0 (tr_bbac30367df9). Every cartservice outbound call therefore pays a constant ~300ms toll: Redis egress spans (HGET, HMSET) cluster tightly at 300-307ms with nothing between the sub-millisecond baseline and 300ms, the penalty multiplies exactly by the number of egress calls per handler (~301ms for single-egress GetCart, ~603ms for two-egress AddItem), and in-process handler time remains under ~1ms (tr_8bf12cc31348). The failure is a wait, not a fault: cartservice's error ratio is flat zero across the whole window with no gaps (tr_06e83135c0b3, tr_789c1de8dfa1) and its logs show only successful handler activity, with add/get pairing stretching from milliseconds to about a second by 03:59-04:00 (tr_5f66d89c5b74). The alerts on frontend, checkoutservice and loadgenerator are the same delay surfacing upstream — checkoutservice makes two cart-facing legs per PlaceOrder and accumulates ~1.2s each, while non-cart spans stay in the 0-19ms range (tr_8bf12cc31348) — and frontend has no change of its own to explain it (tr_685c90555df7). The mechanism is injected delay on a dependency call path, so the fix is to remove the shaping rule, not to redeploy or restart anything.
verdict.reasoning: Three independent signals converge. (1) A discrete change with a concrete latency-injecting mechanism landed ~3 minutes before the first alert (tr_bbac30367df9). (2) The trace shape matches that mechanism precisely rather than merely coinciding with it: a quantized ~300ms floor with no intermediate values, linear scaling with egress-call count, and negligible in-process time (tr_8bf12cc31348). A queueing, GC, saturation or cache-degradation story would produce a spread and a tail; this is a step function. (3) The absence of errors everywhere in cartservice (tr_06e83135c0b3, tr_789c1de8dfa1) and the absence of any dependency-failure line in the logs (tr_5f66d89c5b74) rule out the error-shaped explanations — hard dependency failure, retry amplification, circuit-breaking, load-shedding, crash-and-reschedule. Note the corpus trap the past incidents record: cartservice's flat-zero error rate was twice read as evidence cart was healthy. Here it is the opposite — zero errors plus multi-hundred-millisecond spans is the signature of a service that is waiting, not failing. Classification: a change record is evidence for a class, not the class. The running artifact is correct, so this is not bad_deploy; no configuration value inside cartservice names a wrong address, limit or credential, so this is not bad_config; nothing is exhausted. What the service is doing wrong now is waiting on a slowed egress path, which is dependency_latency, and it stops when the shaping rule is withdrawn — a revert of the injected change rather than a rollback of any release.
open_questions: No latency percentile, CPU, memory or connection-pool metrics were ever retrieved for cartservice (tr_06e83135c0b3, tr_789c1de8dfa1); the ~300ms step is established from traces alone and was never corroborated by a quantile series showing a clean step at 03:54.

The traces show additional ~300ms multiples consumed on the callers' egress paths — frontend's client span ~603ms against a ~301ms cart server span, checkoutservice's ~1204-1222ms against ~301ms (tr_8bf12cc31348). Whether the shaping was applied to more than the cart-service namespace, or whether the delay is being paid on both request and response legs, is unresolved and changes the scope of the fix.
checkoutservice's change history was never queried (tr_685c90555df7 covered frontend only), so a second concurrent injection or change on that side is not excluded.

Log coverage is truncated: roughly 03:47:38-03:59:35 was not returned and the window stops at 04:02:30 rather than 04:05 (tr_5f66d89c5b74), so the absence of errors is confirmed only for the head and tail, not the middle of the incident.

Cart-get entries near 03:59-04:00 carry an empty user identifier, a pattern absent earlier (tr_5f66d89c5b74). No dispatch explained this; it may be a benign artifact of timed-out or retried upstream sessions, or a separate correctness issue riding alongside the latency.
Redis itself was never examined directly. The uniform quantum makes an intrinsic Redis problem unlikely, but no evidence confirms the backing store is healthy underneath the injected delay.

The intent and lifetime of the platform-automation change are unknown — whether it is a scheduled chaos experiment with its own expiry, a traffic-management action, or an unintended attachment. This determines whether removal is safe to do unilaterally and whether it will recur.
